title: Parvati holds her mind on Shiva
hookLine: a stranger mocks the god Parvati has chosen, and her mind doesn't move
carry: dharana: the mind held on one beloved form

cards: After Kama burned, Parvati didn't give up. If beauty couldn't reach Shiva, she would reach him another way. She left her father's palace for the mountains and began tapas, austerity, her whole mind set on Shiva.
Summer heat, winter water, rain. In time she stopped eating even fallen leaves, and people called her Aparna, the one without a leaf.
Then one day a young ascetic with matted hair walks into her hermitage, and starts to talk.

teach.h: THE STRANGER MOCKS SHIVA. PARVATI WON'T HEAR IT.
teach.b: He's charming, and he's sure she's wasting herself. Shiva? the stranger says, in Kalidasa's telling. He haunts cremation grounds, wears snakes, rides an old bull, and nobody knows his birth.
Parvati's answer is fierce: you don't know him, and I won't hear another word. She turns to leave. And the stranger catches her hand: it's Shiva himself.

teach.h: IT WAS SHIVA: 'I'M YOURS, WON BY YOUR TAPAS.'
teach.b: From today, he says, I'm yours, won by your tapas. Hindus tell this as the road to the wedding of Shiva and Parvati, and many teachers read it as a picture of a mind that has found its place and won't be pried away.
Patanjali has a word for that.

teach.h: DHARANA: THE MIND HELD TO ONE PLACE.
teach.b: The third chapter of the Yoga Sutras opens with dharana, in paraphrase: the binding of the mind to a place. The word comes from the root dhri, to hold, the same root as dharma.
The next sutra names what grows from it: dhyana, meditation, when attention flows to that place unbroken. And what should the place be?
Vyasa's commentary names the navel, the tip of the nose, or an outer object, and in the first chapter Patanjali adds, in paraphrase: or by meditating on whatever one finds agreeable.
That leaves room for what so many Hindus already do: hold the mind on their own chosen form of God, their ishta devata: Krishna, Shiva, the Goddess, Ganesha.

teach.h: TRATAKA IS DHARANA YOU CAN SEE.
teach.b: Trataka is dharana you can see. The flame, the mark or the beloved image sits right there, and when the mind wanders, you walk it back. Parvati didn't hold on by force.
She held on because she loved what she was holding.

how: In yoga traditions that follow Patanjali, trataka is taught as a training in dharana, holding attention on a single chosen object; many Hindus choose an image of their ishta devata, their chosen form of God, while others use a flame, a mark or a flower.

o: a still gaze that ties the mind to one place
a gaze that lets the mind roam where it likes
meditating with eyes shut on a word or a sound

games.q: holding the mind — tap the pairs.
p: the mind bound to one place
Parvati, who gave up even leaves
your own chosen form of God

s: Patanjali says the object of concentration must be a flame
in the first chapter he offers meditating on whatever one finds agreeable.
when the stranger mocked Shiva, Parvati defended him and turned to leave
and the stranger was Shiva himself: from today, he said, I'm yours, won by your tapas.
dharana and dhyana are two words for the same thing
dharana is the tying to one place; dhyana is when attention flows there without a break.

games.q: a stranger tells Parvati the god she's chosen isn't worth it. what does she do?
o: argues all night until he gives in.
defends Shiva, won't hear more, and turns to leave.
games.why: her mind stays where she set it. that's dharana: the mind held to one place, and Patanjali allows whatever one finds agreeable, even a beloved form.

practice: Choose your place: if you pray, a picture of the form of God you love; if not, a candle safely lit, a mark on the wall or a flower. Set it at eye level and rest the eyes on it.
When the mind wanders, notice it, and walk it back without scolding, the way Parvati turned back to Shiva season after season. If the eyes tire, close them and keep the form in mind.

wordCard.voice: Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, dharana you can see: the mind held on one place, or one beloved form.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dharana, concentration, holding. In the Yoga Sutras, the mind bound to one place.

carryVoice: Your line: dharana, the mind held on one beloved form. A week of resolve, gathering and gaze. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Parvati Khanda
